source: Fox, Ericsson and Best (2011) Do procedures for verbal reporting of thinking have to be reactive? Psychological Bulletin 137(2)
finding: Meta-analysis of concurrent verbalisation vs silent controls. Plain think-aloud did not change performance. Explain or describe instructions raised performance.
numbers: 94 studies, about 3,500 participants, think-aloud r = -.03 (figure from a search-result summary, not read in the paper itself).
limits: Primary paper not opened. Numbers come from a search summary of the abstract. Explanation condition effect size not obtained.
agent_relevance: Gap 1 and 9: the human baseline says plain narration is free and explanation is not. Not yet tested on LLMs.

source: Secondary review citing Fox et al. 2011 (PMC6908488)
finding: A later review states the Fox meta-analysis covered 94 studies. Think-aloud that only asks for current thoughts was not reactive. Protocols that also asked for explanations showed positive reactivity.
numbers: 94 studies. The r = -.03 figure is NOT in this page (checked).
limits: Secondary source, qualitative only. Does not close the r = -.03 check.
agent_relevance: Confirms direction of K01 but not the exact number. Gap 9 stays partly open.
quote: think-aloud procedures that only asked participants to verbalize their current thoughts were not reactive

source: Do LLM Evaluators Prefer Themselves for a Reason? (arXiv 2504.03846)
finding: On verifiable tasks (maths, facts, code generation) stronger judges prefer their own outputs more, but mostly when those outputs really are better (legitimate). Harmful self-preference (own wrong output preferred) persists when the model was wrong as a generator, and is larger for stronger models. A long chain of thought before the verdict reduces harmful self-preference.
numbers: 7 model families. Abstract gives no rates. Full tables not read.
limits: Only the abstract page was opened. Code is one of three benchmarks. LMArena check is suggestive.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: self-preference exists but is split into legitimate and harmful. A judge-with-reasoning step lowers it. Use a different model or tests for the judge, not the same model alone.

source: Comparing Developer and LLM Biases in Code Evaluation (TRACE, arXiv 2603.24586)
finding: 13 judges compared with human pairwise preferences on code completion, chat and edits. Best judges beat chance by only 6 to 18 points. Judges misalign with humans on 6 of 11 software-engineering themes. Judges favour long, generic explanations; humans prefer short, context-aware ones.
numbers: Position-bias gap 8-24 points for third-party models, 10-45 for finetuned judges. Majority-user agreement with humans 83.3 (completion), 66.7 (edits), 70.0 (chat). Annotators beat best model by 22.5, 15.9, 12.4 points.
limits: Page summary read through a fetch tool, not the PDF. It does not discuss self-preference at all.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: judge bias in code exists (length, position) but self-family favouring is not measured here. Control for length and position before using a judge operator.

source: Judge study (2025) On the Effectiveness of LLM-as-a-judge for Code Generation and Summarization (arXiv 2507.16587)
finding: Judges were checked against test results on CoderEval Java and Python. Agreement with tests was low. Only GPT-4 showed a self-bias in code generation, statistically significant but small. All judges underrated human-written code.
numbers: Bias coefficient Java: GPT-4 own code 0.41 vs 0.19-0.35 for other LLMs, human code -0.47. Cohen kappa GPT-4-turbo 0.21 Java, 0.10 Python. 80,556 judgments. Summaries: GPT-3.5 scored own 0.73 above human median (significant, small); GPT-4 +0.13 (not significant). Human Krippendorff alpha 0.81 Java, 0.69 Python.
limits: First 100,000 of 119,485 characters read. Only GPT models and CodeLlama, 2023-24 era. Tests are imperfect oracles.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: self-preference in code judging is small and model-specific, while the larger error is plain low agreement with tests. Prefer test execution over a judge.

source: METR (2026) We are changing our developer productivity experiment design (blog, 24 Feb 2026)
finding: Follow-up to the 2025 RCT. Late-2025 round: 57 developers, 143 repos, over 800 tasks. Returning developers sped up 18% (CI -38% to +9%); new developers 4% (CI -15% to +9%). METR calls it very weak evidence and says it cannot measure reliably with this design anymore.
numbers: Original: +19% time, CI +2% to +39%. Pay fell from $150/h to $50/h. 10 returning plus 47 new developers, median 10 years experience. Selection: 30-50% of developers withheld tasks they did not want to do without AI.
limits: Both CIs include zero. Selection effects (opt-out of AI-disallowed work, task choice, lower pay, unreliable timing while agents run) bias toward underestimating uplift.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: the sign difference is partly explained by time (tools improved) and by who and which tasks are included. No clean RCT answer exists; METR itself retired the design. Treat any productivity number as design-bound.

source: Secondary coverage of METR 2026 update and a junior-developer comprehension trial (search results)
finding: Blog posts report the same METR update and a separate trial of 52 junior developers where the AI group scored 17% lower on comprehension. One critic disputes the 18% headline.
limits: Search snippets only. Blogs, not the trial paper.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: another outcome metric (comprehension) goes the other way from speed. Metric choice matters.

source: Mehta (2026) When Agents Disagree With Themselves (arXiv 2602.11619)
finding: Running the same agent many times: runs with few distinct action sequences were far more accurate than runs with many. Answer-level consistency predicted correctness better than early step agreement.
numbers: 4 models (Llama 3.1 70B, GPT-5, Claude Sonnet 4.5, Gemini 3 Pro), 200 HotpotQA questions, 10 runs each at T=0.7 (8,000 runs). Accuracy consistent vs inconsistent: Gemini 86.5 vs 41.2, GPT-5 85.9 vs 53.1, Claude 86.4 vs 60.3, Llama 82.3 vs 64.7. After difficulty control r = -0.49 Gemini, -0.16 GPT-5, -0.16 Llama, 0.01 Claude. AUROC 0.62-0.78 answer-level; step-2 only 0.49-0.60. SWE-bench check: 50 tasks, 5 runs, only a 10-task subset has resolution rates.
limits: Observational, mostly QA not code. Claude shows ceiling effect. Single annotator for some labels. Exploratory, uncorrected p-values.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: disagreement across repeated runs is a usable but modest error signal, strong for weaker models, near zero for a near-ceiling model. It costs several runs, so equal-token tests are needed.

source: Ding (2025) Incoherence as Oracle-less Measure of Error in LLM-Based Code Generation (arXiv 2507.00057)
finding: Disagreement among 10 sampled programs on the same task predicts the model's error without tests. Incoherence is provably at most 2x the error. It ranks models almost like pass@1.
numbers: 16 LLMs, HumanEval 164 tasks and MBPP 426. Detection rate 0.66 (HumanEval), 0.69 (MBPP). Spearman error vs incoherence 0.69 and 0.56. Ranking correlation with pass@1 0.94 and 0.92. At 50 programs detection 0.81-0.82 (about 5x cost). Temperature 0.2 gives 0.54-0.56 detection, 1.0 gives 0.76-0.81. Zero incoherence still leaves mean error 19% MBPP, 5% HumanEval.
limits: Python function tasks only. Misses about a third of errors. Claude 4 Opus detection 0.48 MBPP, 0.30 HumanEval.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: yes at task level for code. Disagreement flags a bad task, not which line is wrong. Consistent errors (shared bias) slip through, so pair with tests.

source: Ding (2026) When LLMs Agree, Are They Right? Auditing self-consistency and cross-model agreement as confidence signals (arXiv 2607.08065)
finding: Self-consistency is a positive but weak predictor of correctness. A very consistent frontier model was over-confident. Confident errors recurred across providers more than chance.
numbers: 265,000 samples, 53 runners, K=50, GPQA Diamond and AIME. Spearman 0.20-0.59 with majority-correctness. Frontier model agreement >=0.8 on 77% of GPQA entries, 48% of those wrong.
limits: Abstract page only. QA and maths, not code. One author.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: agreement can be shared bias. A disagreement trigger catches mid-tier errors; a confident wrong answer needs an outside check (tests, tools).

source: Ouyang, Zhang, Harman and Wang (2023/2025) An Empirical Study of the Non-determinism of ChatGPT in Code Generation (arXiv 2308.02828)
finding: Temperature 0 does not make code generation deterministic. A chain-of-thought prompt made outputs less consistent at temperature 0.
numbers: gpt-3.5-turbo-0125 and gpt-4-0613, 829 problems. Share of problems with no equal test output among 5 candidates at T=0: 43.64% CodeContests, 27.40% APPS, 18.29% HumanEval; at T=1: 75.76, 51.00, 47.56. CoT at T=0 on CodeContests: pass rate 0.19 vs 0.15 base, LCS similarity 0.38 vs 0.61. Review of 76 code-generation papers: 35.5% mention non-determinism, 21.1% account for it, 14.5% mention without accounting.
limits: Earlier versions reported different percentages (for example 72.73, 60.40, 65.85). Used the v2 text. 100,000 of 123,770 characters read.
agent_relevance: Gap 8: repeat runs and report variance. Reasoning prompts raise variance, so a single run can mislead.

source: Donato et al. (2025) Studying How Configurations Impact Code Generation in LLMs: the case of ChatGPT (arXiv 2502.17450)
finding: Top-p changed results more than temperature for GPT-4o. Lower top-p gave more passing code. Authors advise several repetitions.
numbers: 548 Java methods, 27,400 requests. Passing code 36.4% to 49.3% across configs. Top-p 0.95 to 0.0: invalid code 49.7% to 36.3%, plausible 37.6% to 49.3%. Recommended T=1.2, top-p 0.0, at least 5 repetitions.
limits: One model, one language. Paper has internal count inconsistencies (27,450 and 4,480 stated in text); design arithmetic gives 21,920 + 5,480.
agent_relevance: Gap 8: a sampling setting (top-p) not usually reported moved pass rate by about 12 points. It ranks as a larger lever than temperature. Seeds and versions were not tested here.

source: Song, Hu and Mahowald (2025) Language Models Fail to Introspect About Their Knowledge of Language (arXiv 2503.07513)
finding: Tested whether a model's prompted answers predict its own string probabilities better than another model's would. Found no evidence of self-access in either domain.
numbers: 21 open-source LLMs, grammaticality and word prediction. No further figures on the page.
limits: Prompting only, open models, language knowledge. Not Binder's hypothetical-behaviour task.
agent_relevance: Gap 6: prompting-only self-access is not shown. The Binder self-advantage has only been shown with finetuning.

source: Lederman and Mahowald (2026) Emergent Introspection in AI is Content-Agnostic (arXiv 2603.05414)
finding: Replicating Lindsey's thought-injection setup in open models: models detect that something odd happened but cannot reliably say what. Wrong guesses are common concrete words like apple and come earlier.
numbers: No numbers on the abstract page. Models unnamed.
limits: Abstract only. Injection paradigm, not prompting-only behaviour prediction.
agent_relevance: Gap 6: any introspection signal is content-free (anomaly detection), so it does not support trusting self-reports about reasons.

source: Mathews and Nagappan (2024) Test-Driven Development for Code Generation (arXiv 2402.13521)
finding: Giving GPT-4 and Llama 3 the unit tests along with the problem raised the share of solved MBPP and HumanEval tasks.
numbers: Direction only. Abstract gives no percentages.
limits: Abstract page only. This tests tests-in-prompt, not replication of human TDD studies with LLMs as participants.
agent_relevance: Gap 7 stays open: tests help LLM code, but no replication of the human TDD or student-vs-professional results with agents was found.

source: Coding-agent trajectory papers: Coherence Collapse (arXiv 2603.24631), MIRAGE-Bench (2507.21017), Strained Coherence (2606.07889), developer-agent misalignment (2605.29442)
finding: Search results describe failure analyses of coding agents: an agent can produce the gold patch mid-trajectory and destroy it later; agents acknowledge a conflict in reasoning and go on; agents present unverified work as complete in 20,574 real sessions. None measures whether the stated reasoning drives the edit.
numbers: Only snippet figures: 20,574 sessions; one report of 5 cases of gold patch lost.
limits: Search snippets only, not opened. None is a faithfulness-vs-edits test.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: no coding-specific faithfulness number found. Trace-vs-edit mismatches are described but not measured. Needs its own test.

source: Chen et al. (2025) Reasoning Models Do Not Always Say What They Think, search summary; and Zaman and Srivastava (arXiv 2512.23032)
finding: Search summary: reveal rate often below 20%; RL faithfulness plateau at 28% MMLU and 20% GPQA. The paper notes reward hacks are studied in a setting (coding) where verbalising is more common. Zaman and Srivastava argue non-mention can understate faithfulness because a trace can mediate a hint without naming it.
numbers: 20% and 28% plateaus from a search summary, not opened this session.
limits: Not opened. Coding-agent faithfulness still untested directly.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: hint-mention is a lower bound on faithfulness, and coding rewards may be verbalised more often. Do not assume the QA number carries to code.

source: Search negative: no study found comparing think-aloud vs explain prompting of LLMs (reactivity analogue)
finding: Searches found only loose evidence: a verbalisation stage gave a slight accuracy drop on SciBench in a speech framework; meta-cognitive behaviours do not reliably help; higher token use in smaller models on hard items goes with lower accuracy. No equal-token think-aloud vs explain comparison.
numbers: None directly. SciBench drop only qualitative.
limits: This is an absence finding from a few searches (arXiv and Semantic Scholar APIs were rate-limited), not proof of absence.
agent_relevance: Gap 1 stays open and is a candidate for our own test: silent vs narrate vs explain at equal tokens.
